title: The shipwreck (Acts 27–28)
hook: two weeks of storm, Paul breaks bread on deck, 276 swim to Malta, and a viper bites harmlessly

segments.voice: Yesterday, unknown god: Paul at the altar in Athens, quoting the poets on their own hill.

Some weeks are all storm, and you can't see the sky. Now board a cargo ship in the Mediterranean, late in the sailing season. Paul is aboard as a prisoner, not a passenger, taken to Rome for trial under a Roman officer named Julius. Paul warns it's too late in the year to sail. Nobody listens. Then a violent wind sweeps off Crete; the ship is caught and can't turn into it. They lash ropes around the hull to hold it together, throw the cargo overboard, then the ship's gear. Day after day, no sun, no stars. Luke, writing as we, as if aboard, says all hope that we should be saved was taken away.
screen: `A PRISONER ON A CARGO SHIP.` → `THE WIND OFF CRETE.` → `NO SUN, NO STARS.`

segments.voice: Paul stands among the exhausted crew: in the King James Bible, "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." An angel stood by me last night, he says. Again: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God." Be of good cheer is the King James wording; the Greek means something like be good-spirited. Take heart. On the fourteenth night they sense land. Some sailors try to slip away in the lifeboat, and are stopped. Before dawn, everyone starving and terrified, Paul does something ordinary: tells them to eat. Two weeks without a real meal, he says; this is for your health. Then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." Took, gave thanks, broke: Luke's words for anamnesis, now on a storm-battered deck, among soldiers, sailors and prisoners. All take heart and eat; Luke counts two hundred and seventy-six people. At daybreak the ship runs aground and breaks apart. Swimmers jump first; the rest float in on planks. Every one reaches the shore. It's Malta; the islanders build a fire in the cold rain. A viper comes out of the firewood and fastens onto Paul's hand. The locals decide he must be a murderer. He shakes it into the fire, nothing happens, and they change their minds: he must be a god.
screen: `BE OF GOOD CHEER.` · `THIS IS FOR YOUR HEALTH.` · `HE TOOK BREAD, AND GAVE THANKS.` · `276, ALL SAFE TO LAND.` · then, large: `TAKE HEART.`

segments.voice: If you have something near, bread, a cracker, fruit, a cup of tea, hold it before you eat; if not, picture it. If you pray, give thanks for it, as Paul did; if not, notice where it came from, and how many hands it passed through. Then eat slowly, like someone who hasn't eaten in a while, and let it steady you, one bite at a time.
The shipwreck. Fourteen days of storm, bread broken on a storm-battered deck, and two hundred and seventy-six people safe on Malta.
Your line: take heart. Next, Paul's letters as real mail. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians give thanks before meals, as Paul does on the deck. In Malta, Paul's shipwreck is remembered every February 10 with a public holiday and feast, and Maltese tradition traces the island's faith to it.

original.note: Greek: be of good spirit, take heart. Paul says it twice on the ship (Acts 27:22, 25).

trapdoor: what you thought: an adventure story with a snake at the end.
what it means: in the worst of the storm, a prisoner tells everyone to take heart, and to eat, and breaks bread on the deck.
what a scholar hears: Luke writes it as we, as if on board, and describes the bread with the words of the Last Supper: took, gave thanks, broke.
recall: from martys: at first, a witness

chat.says: In the storm, what did Paul do that helped everyone on board?
options: He told them to take heart and eat, then gave thanks and broke bread before them.
He took over steering the ship himself once the sailors had all given up.
He calmed the wind with a prayer, just as Jesus had once done on the lake.
chat.meaning: Paul said be of good cheer: for I believe God. Then he took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and all took heart and ate.

Malta.meaning: the island where everyone came safely ashore

Crete.meaning: the island the violent wind swept them away from

Julius.meaning: the Roman officer taking Paul to Rome

viper.meaning: a snake that came out of the firewood

notes: The 'we' passages: the script says Luke writes 'as if he's on board'; tradition names Luke as the companion, and scholars debate it. Confirm phrasing.
276 (Acts 27:37): some manuscripts read a different number (e.g., 76); KJV and most texts read 276.
Feast of Saint Paul's Shipwreck in Malta, February 10, a public holiday; confirm.
The eucharistic echo (took, gave thanks, broke) is widely noted; churches differ on whether this meal was a Eucharist. Not claimed in the script.
